title: Section 13B HMA — Divorce by mutual consent

content.overview: Section 13B permits divorce by mutual consent where both parties have been living separately for a period of one year or more, have not been able to live together, and have mutually agreed that the marriage should be dissolved; the court may, after the statutory cooling-off and on being satisfied, grant a decree.
content.study: File a joint petition; after presentation there is ordinarily a six-month cooling-off before the second motion, which must be completed within eighteen months of the first petition unless waived by the court in appropriate cases. Consent must continue until the decree; either party may withdraw consent before the decree. Contrast with contested divorce under section 13 and link to sections 24 and 25 for interim and permanent financial relief.

learningObjectives: Explain Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 Section 13b and its statutory purpose.
Identify and apply the provision's ingredients to a factual problem.
Distinguish the provision from related HMA remedies.
enhancement.definition: Section 13B provides for divorce by mutual consent when both spouses satisfy the statutory requirements and continue to make the required joint motion with mutual consent.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Mutual consent is a jurisdictional fact. The court must be satisfied about the statutory conditions and continuing consent before granting the decree.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, Section 13B(1) and (2), subject to the Supreme Court's interpretation concerning waiver of the waiting period in appropriate cases.
essentialIngredients: Living separately for at least one year immediately preceding presentation.
Mutual agreement that the marriage should be dissolved.
Second motion within the statutory framework unless lawfully waived.
Court satisfaction after hearing the parties and inquiry.
Continuing mutual consent until decree under the settled rule.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 13B differs fundamentally from contested divorce. The petition itself does not dissolve the marriage. The statutory second-motion mechanism and continuing consent are central. The Supreme Court has held that mutual consent is a jurisdictional fact and has also recognized that the six-month period may be waived in appropriate exceptional circumstances.
examples: Two spouses who have lived separately for the statutory period file a joint Section 13B petition. Before the decree, one withdraws consent. The court cannot simply treat the original consent as sufficient to grant a mutual-consent decree.
enhancement.distinctions: Section 13B requires mutual consent; Section 13 requires proof of a statutory matrimonial ground. Section 13B's six-month period is subject to judicial waiver in appropriate cases.

caseLaw.name: Hitesh Bhatnagar v. Deepa Bhatnagar
caseLaw.citation: Civil Appeal No. 6288 of 2008; Supreme Court judgment
caseLaw.holding: The Supreme Court held that mutual consent under Section 13B is a jurisdictional fact and that one party may withdraw consent before the decree; it also reaffirmed the continuing-consent rule from Sureshta Devi.

caseLaw.name: Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur
caseLaw.holding: The Supreme Court held that the six-month period under Section 13B(2) can be waived by the court in appropriate exceptional circumstances when the statutory objectives have otherwise been met.
caseLaw.relevance: Direct authority for waiver of the Section 13B cooling-off period.

enhancement.problemApplication: Check the separation period, inability to live together, agreement, first petition, second motion, continuing consent and any application for waiver before determining whether a decree can be passed.
